result.process_description:
Title: Car Service

The police has a new app to remind you of your car service.
The process is started after a successful service.
When a service is necessary, the system checks if your car is still registered.
If it is registered, you are notified.
If you do not go to the service, you are fined after 30 days.
At the car service facility the mechanic enters the problems of your car for reference.
While you wait (can take several days), you get status updates via email.
You can pay through the app, when the repair is done.
The mechanic enters that the repair was successful and you got your "Pickerl".
The mechanic enters the time for you next service.

result.rule: Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.
Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Use message events for directed participant communication, signal events for broadcasts, and timer events for stated dates, durations or cycles.

result.rule: When the description states, in one sentence, several items that the same participant enters or selects, joined by commas or 'and', and each item is a distinct input or choice the participant makes: Model each item in that list as its own user task, in the order the sentence states them, and label each task with the verb and the single item it covers, taken from the description. Do not combine two items into one task label, and do not drop any item from the list.

When the description has a participant perform two or more of its own actions on the same item in one sentence, joined by a conjunction such as 'and', after being told the item is available for it, and the generated model shows only one task or merges them into a state label: Model each action the participant performs on the item as its own task, in the order the sentence gives, after the wait for the stated availability. Label each task with the action the description states (for example, the participant takes the item, then the participant uses it). Do not merge them into one task, and do not use a catch event or an end event to stand for the action.

When the description states that a named actor performs an action that is part of the process, such as submitting a request or signing up: Model that action as a task whose label keeps the actor and the action verb and object as written in the description, for example 'Actor verb object', rather than a shortened verb-object label that drops the actor. Keep the task after the start event that the description implies, and do not replace it with a separate start event or a user task that repeats the actor's action.

When the description states, within a single clause, several distinct actions by one participant joined by commas, 'and' or 'or' (for example, in the sentence that states the outcome of the process, where one action changes a participant's status and another is a separate commitment): Model each named action in that clause as its own task, in the order the description states, each with a short verb-object label taken from the description. Do not merge the actions into one task label and do not drop any of them. When the clause states the outcome, place these tasks in sequence before the end event, and let the end event name only the outcome reached.
